extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, referees, academic researchers, and science-policy scholars interested in peer-review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative dimensions for assessing journal peer-review systems, referee reports, and editorial practices (including proposals such as optional published refereeing and open commentary). Useful for editors, reviewers, and researchers studying peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception-of-author_status_and_credibility_bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias deriving solely from the perception of authors' status and credibility, as judged from their name and institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peters & Ceci show that bias can remain when cognitive-relativist explanations are implausible; reviewers may favor or disfavor manuscripts based on visible author/institution markers even absent substantive differences in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared_training_or_cognitive_relativism_bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees trained in similar institutional/cognitive settings tend to respond favorably to certain methodological, theoretical, or expressive aspects of manuscripts from similarly trained authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (e.g., Crane; Gordon 1980) attribute elevated favorable evaluations when author and referee share institutional group membership to higher consensus on research beliefs within groups; this is distinct from status-based bias and implies evaluative standards vary with intellectual socialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer_literature_knowledge_and_detection_of_prior_publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of editors and reviewers to recognize that a submitted manuscript has already been published or to detect relevant prior literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peters & Ceci found many previously published papers were not detected; failure to detect redundancy undermines filtering and suggests reviewers/editors should be assessed on familiarity with recent issues of target journals and core literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy_and_constructiveness_of_referee_reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should be accurate, comment on important issues, and give fair recommendations; reports vary widely in quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horrobincategory: ~1/3 of reports are accurate and fair, ~1/3 accurate but obsessed with trivialities, ~1/3 inaccurate and demonstrably so. Evaluation should consider factual correctness, relevance of criticisms, and fairness of recommendation (accept/revise/reject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone_and_language_of_reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports should avoid intemperate language and inflammatory phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horrobin notes frequent intemperate language in reports; evaluators should penalize unnecessarily abrasive tone as it harms scientific discourse and can reflect poor professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjudge_reliability_of_evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which different referees agree about a manuscript's acceptability, quality, or relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings suggest low agreement (judges share, at best, ~50% variance). Measures of system performance should report interrater agreement and recognize that acceptability, quality, and relevance are distinct targets of judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role_of_refereeing_as_certification_and_communication_function
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing serves both to filter/certify knowledge and to contribute indirectly to scientific communication and the structure of what is presented for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Griffith and others argue referees act like 'certifiers' (Zuckerman & Merton); evaluation of refereeing systems should account for both direct report content and indirect systemic effects (e.g., what gets written, submitted, or pursued).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_methodological_criticism_and_wastebasket_risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological inadequacy is often cited as grounds for rejection but can be a matter of degree and may function as a 'wastebasket' category when other grounds are lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hogan warns that methodological critique can be overused to reject unconventional or marginal work; assessments should distinguish substantive methodological flaws from dismissive or dogmatic methodism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection_rate_is_not_a_valid_proxy_for_quality
rubrics_metrics.description: High rejection rates do not guarantee that accepted manuscripts are measurably better than rejected ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peters & Ceci and commentators note that focusing on rejection-rate as a quality indicator is misleading; evaluation of journal quality should use direct measures of content quality or impact rather than rejection percentage alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional_published_refereeing_policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed system allowing authors the option to publish a manuscript accompanied by the anonymous unanswered comments of the referee (without author rebuttal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. A. Gordon proposes this as a way to reduce undue weight of poor reports while preserving refereeing; features include author responsibility for deciding to publish, retention of referee anonymity (essential when publishing critical reports), possible publication of referee names in low-stakes cases, and optional journal-level restrictions (subject matter, frequency, form of comments). It can be implemented without changing existing review procedures and is intended for cases with substantial referee-author disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee_anonymity_for_published_comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity of referees is essential when publishing their critical comments alongside a contested manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity permits referees to argue freely without fear of personal controversy and forces subsequent discussion to focus on disputed points rather than referee identity; journals choosing optional published refereeing should preserve anonymity in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open_peer_commentary_vs_optional_published_refereeing_distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer commentary (as used by BBS) is a complementary system distinct from optional published refereeing: it is accorded only to refereed, accepted articles with commentators identified and formal author responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should recognize the functional differences: open commentary supplements accepted work with signed debate; optional published refereeing makes contested manuscripts and anonymous criticisms public without author rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness_of_blind_and_other_systemic_reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Systemic changes (double-blind reviewing, public abstracts of all submissions, removal of anonymity, mandatory published rebuttals) have variable and limited effectiveness in eliminating poor or incorrect referee reports and may have trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benwell, Carta, Robertsen, Kumar, and others are cited: double-blind can increase acceptance of underrepresented groups (example: women), but such peripheral changes do not necessarily reduce incidence of poor reports; some measures may compromise the refereeing system's effectiveness if they overcorrect (e.g., remove useful accountability or reduce referee candor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees_contribute_to_manuscript_quality_through_comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee comments often make significant contributions to improving manuscripts and authors welcome substantive reviews for making improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korten & Griffith and anecdotal reports show authors value constructive feedback; evaluation of refereeing should reward constructive, detailed, and improvement-oriented reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer_selection_and_availability_as_quality_metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of reviewers (e.g., younger/newer reviewers having more time and providing more detailed reviews) affect review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honig notes that younger/newer individuals often make the best reviewers because they can devote more effort; journals should consider reviewer workload, incentives, and selection policies when assessing review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial_practice_of_sharing_reports_among_referees_and_with_authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sending each referee's report to the author and to the other referees as a routine practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hartley suggests wider use of this practice; it can increase transparency among referees, promote convergence, and provide authors fuller information about the range of concerns raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_independent_paid_consultants_as_auxiliary_evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal that authors might commission independent consultants (paid reviewers) to evaluate papers prior to journal submission, with such consultants' remarks submitted with the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honig suggests paid consultants could provide a focused, funded evaluation; journals could accept manuscripts accompanied by consultant reports as supplementary evidence of quality, though this raises equity and access considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core_scientific_constraints_for_evaluating_submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three fundamental constraints for assessing scientific proposals: (a) logical consistency, (b) testability, (c) being subject to ongoing self-corrective discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honig cites these as minimal criteria for evaluating speculative or paradigm-challenging submissions; abstract logical problems are insufficient without prospect of empirical confirmation and engagement in corrective discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias_against_highly_innovative_work
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review tends to be built on the assumption that peers are equal and will recognize genius; in practice ordinary scientists often fail to recognize and may reject highly innovative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horrobin argues the system is philosophically faulty in that it systematically disfavors exceptional, paradigm-shifting contributions; evaluative frameworks should include safeguards to reduce conservatism against innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need_for_more_research_on_peer_review_and_publication_process
rubrics_metrics.description: A call for broader research into peer reviewing and the whole process of writing and publishing scientific papers, beyond single-method small-scale studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commentators urge diverse strategies and broader focus (editorial practices, publication formats, new technologies) to obtain valid, generalizable evidence about what works in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability_measures_for_referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for increasing referee accountability such as publishing referee names at the end of accepted manuscripts or optional publication of anonymous referee comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals wishing to provide modest accountability could publish referee names for accepted papers; alternatively, optional published refereeing gives accountability via public exposure of reviewer arguments (while anonymity may be maintained when necessary). Editors should weigh accountability benefits against risks to referee candor and willingness to review.
